extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, patent litigators, and jurors in U.S. design patent trials (IPO members and courts)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for United States design patent litigation covering what a design patent is, claim construction, infringement (direct and indirect), invalidity grounds, burdens of proof, evidence rules, damages (including §289 profits), and jury procedures. Intended as templates courts and counsel can use or adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: What a design patent protects (ornamental design)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent is directed to the ornamental design for an article of manufacture. 'Ornamental design' means the shape of the design, and/or the surface decoration on the design. A valid U.S. design patent gives the patent owner the right for 14 years from the date the patent is granted to prevent others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the patented design within the United States or importing it into the United States without the patent holder’s permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains prosecution basics: application includes a specification with drawings/photographs and a single claim that refers to the drawings; examiner reviews prior art to determine if claimed design is patentable. Cited authority: 35 U.S.C. § 171.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (novelty and non-obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining a design patent application, the examiner considers whether the claim defines a design that is new and not obvious in view of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art is defined by law and includes things publicly known, publicly used in the U.S., patented or described in a publication before the creation of the claimed design. The prosecution history and references cited by the PTO are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (scope and content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art generally includes things that existed before the claimed design and might typically be a patent or a printed publication, public use, public display, or offers for sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further detailed in anticipation and obviousness sections (e.g., public use, prior patents, printed publications, commercial use, foreign patents, one-year bars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope defined by the drawings (overall visual impression)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claim is defined by the drawing(s) in the design patent, not just by one feature. The scope encompasses its visual appearance as a whole and in particular the overall visual impression it creates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all features of the design as a whole, not isolated portions. The specification supplements drawings. The prosecution history may affect the claimed design. Cited authorities include Egyptian Goddess (Fed. Cir. en banc) and Elmer v. ICC Fabricating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid vs. broken lines in drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: All matter depicted in solid lines contributes to the overall appearance of the design and forms part of the claim; any features shown in broken lines and described as disclaimed are excluded from the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to show features in broken lines signals inclusion of such features in the claimed design. (Elmer; In re Blum; Contessa; Durling citations provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: One claim rule and multiple embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent can only have one claim. It is permissible to illustrate more than one embodiment in a single design patent application only if they are directed to substantially the same design and are not patentably distinct from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: 37 C.F.R. § 1.153; Egyptian Goddess; Phillips; Markman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentality (lack of ornamentality as invalidity defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity can be based on lack of ornamentality—i.e., if the claim does not claim an ornamental design for an article of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears among invalidity topics; jury should consider ornamentality as a potential ground for invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — preponderance of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party has the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence, it means the evidence must persuade you that the claim or defense is more probable than not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to most civil issues: e.g., plaintiff bears burden by preponderance that defendant infringed the claim. (Adapted from National Jury Instruction Project.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party has the burden by clear and convincing evidence, it means the evidence has persuaded you that the claim or defense is highly probable; this is a higher standard than preponderance but less than beyond a reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for certain issues such as proving invalidity or willful infringement. Cited authorities given (Pfizer v. Apotex; Intel v. ITC).

rubrics_metrics.name: What is evidence (and what is not)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence consists of sworn testimony of witnesses, exhibits received into evidence, and any facts agreed by the lawyers. Arguments, statements by lawyers, questions/objections, stricken or excluded testimony, and anything seen/heard when court is not in session are not evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawyers' opening/closing statements are for interpretation only; follow limiting instructions when evidence is admitted for limited purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence for limited purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Some evidence may be admitted for a limited purpose only; when so instructed, consider it only for that limited purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the court’s limiting instruction exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs. circumstantial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct evidence is direct proof (e.g., witness testimony about what they personally saw). Circumstantial evidence is proof of facts that permit inference of another fact. The law makes no distinction between the weight to be given to either type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury decides how much weight to give any evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: No transcript available to jury (readback procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors must rely on their recollection of the evidence; a transcript is not provided, but jurors may request readback of selected testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural: jurors may request readback during deliberations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposition testimony in lieu of live testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposition is sworn testimony taken before trial and may be used at trial when a witness is unavailable; it should be considered as if the witness had been present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider deposition testimony the same way as live testimony insofar as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of witnesses (factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding witness credibility, consider: (1) opportunity and ability to perceive; (2) memory; (3) inconsistent prior statements; (4) manner while testifying; (5) interest/bias; (6) contradictory evidence; (7) reasonableness of testimony in light of all evidence; and (8) any other factors bearing on believability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may believe all, part, or none of a witness's testimony; number of witnesses does not determine weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert opinion (weight and evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some witnesses, because of education or experience, may state opinions and reasons for them. Opinion testimony should be judged like any other testimony and may be accepted or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider expert's education and experience, reasons given, and all other evidence in deciding weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — judge's role and acceptance by jury
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the judge's job to provide the meaning of the claim(s) of the asserted design patent(s). The jury must accept the judge's meaning and use it when deciding infringement and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope encompasses visual appearance as a whole; judge will instruct that claim covers what is shown and described. Cited authorities: Markman, Phillips, Egyptian Goddess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — functional features included if shown in solid lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional features illustrated in solid lines are part of the claimed design if they contribute to the overall visual appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if portions perform a function, if depicted in solid lines they contribute to the claimed visual appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — compare accused product to the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding infringement, jurors must compare the defendant’s accused product to the patent (the claim/drawings), not to the plaintiff’s commercial product, unless instructed otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent law gives the owner the right to exclude making/using/offering/selling/importing the patented design during the patent term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct (literal) infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal infringement requires that the accused product falls within the scope of the claimed design as shown in the patent drawings; jury asked whether patent holder has proven infringement more probable than not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model verdict forms ask direct (literal) infringement questions; jury compares accused article to the claimed design as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — inducing infringement (elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove inducing infringement, the patent holder must show (a) the defendant actively encouraged or instructed another person to use a product in a way that infringes the claim, (b) the defendant knew of the design patent at that time, (c) the defendant knew or should have known the encouragement/instructions would result in infringement, and (d) another person actually infringed the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model verdict form B frames these as separate elements to be proven by a preponderance of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — contributory infringement (elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove contributory infringement, the patent holder must show (i) the defendant supplied a part or component to another for use in a product that infringes the claim; (ii) the component was a material part of the infringing product; (iii) the defendant supplied the component with knowledge of the design patent and that the component was especially made or adapted for infringing use; and (iv) the component did not have a substantial non-infringing use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model verdict form B lists these elements; jury decides each by preponderance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement (standard and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful infringement must be proven by clear and convincing evidence (i.e., it must be highly probable). If jury finds willfulness, that decision should not affect the damage award directly; the judge will take willfulness into account later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff bears burden of proving willfulness by clear and convincing evidence. Willfulness is a separate question on verdict forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent is anticipated if, to an ordinary observer, a prior art reference is identical in all material respects to the claimed design. Anticipation can be shown by prior public knowledge/use, prior patents or printed publications, prior U.S. patents/applications, prior U.S. manufacture, prior foreign patent more than one year before U.S. filing, offers for sale/sales more than one year before filing, or if the named inventor did not invent the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model verdict form provides itemized checkboxes identifying different anticipation theories (public use, printed publication, prior patent, sale, foreign patent, one-year bars, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — obviousness (ordinary-observer analysis and factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity can be based on obviousness: whether the claimed design would have been obvious to the ordinary observer at the time the patent application was filed. Consider level of ordinary skill, scope and content of prior art, differences between claimed design and prior art, and secondary considerations indicating nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations include commercial success due to the merits of the claimed design, copying by others, acceptance/praise/licensing. Factors indicating obviousness include independent design by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designer of ordinary skill in the art (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary skill in the art refers to the level of experience, education, and/or training those individuals working in the area of the design ordinarily possessed at the time of the effective filing date of the patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a baseline for obviousness analysis and assessing enablement/understandability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — written description, enablement, and indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity grounds include lack of adequate written description, lack of enablement (i.e., failure to enable a designer of ordinary skill to understand what the claimed design looks like), and indefiniteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model verdict includes specific questions on whether the patent does not enable a designer of ordinary skill to understand the claimed design (clear-and-convincing standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — improper inventorship and double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity can be based on improper inventorship (patent does not list the actual inventors) and on double patenting (features producing the novel aesthetic effect are the same as novel structure claimed in a utility patent/application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model verdict includes separate questions for these defenses; standard is high probability (clear and convincing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unenforceability — inequitable conduct (materiality and intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unenforceability (inequitable conduct) allegations require evaluation of materiality (whether withheld/misrepresented information was material to patentability) and intent to deceive or mislead the PTO; courts balance materiality and intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections list materiality, intent, and balancing; jury may be instructed accordingly with cited authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — types (lost profits and reasonable royalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two primary types of damages are lost profits (compensatory) and reasonable royalty. Jury must determine damages the plaintiff has proven more probable than not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes instructions on when damages/profits begin, burden of proof, elements to prove lost profits, and calculation of reasonable royalty (rate × base).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — factors (Georgia‑Pacific style list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider in determining a reasonable royalty include (non-exhaustive): the royalties customary for similar designs; whether plaintiff and defendant are competitors; commercial success attributable to the patented design; extent and value of defendant’s use of the patented design; advantages of using the patented design over non-patented products; portion of profit due to the patented design versus other factors; and expert opinions about a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapted from Georgia‑Pacific factors and National Jury Instruction Project; jury may weigh competing evidence on these factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional remedy — defendant’s total profit under 35 U.S.C. § 289
rubrics_metrics.description: If plaintiff elects recovery under 35 U.S.C. § 289, and jury finds infringement and the patent is not invalid, plaintiff is to recover the defendant’s total profit attributable to the infringement (i.e., entire profit on sale of the article to which the patented design is applied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total profit excludes profit from other products sold in association. Plaintiff bears burden of proving defendant’s gross revenue; defendant bears burden of proving deductible expenses and portion of profit attributable to factors other than the infringed design. Deductible expenses must have a nexus to the infringing product’s sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages calculation burdens and nexus for expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross revenue is all receipts from using the design in sales of infringing products (plaintiff must prove by preponderance). Expenses (deductible) include cost of goods and other costs directly attributable to sales if there is a nexus between the infringing product and the expense; defendant must prove deductible expenses and non-attributable profit by preponderance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless defendant proves part of profit attributable to other factors, find total profit attributable to infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model verdict form structure and required jury findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Model verdict forms provide structured questions for jurors to answer (e.g., infringement, willfulness, invalidity (various grounds), damages). Verdict must be unanimous and signed by foreperson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two sample forms: Form A (simple) and Form B (detailed with direct/indirect infringement and enumerated invalidity theories). These are offered as starting points for courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury duty, deliberation procedure, and unanimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors must find facts from evidence, apply the law as given by the judge, not be influenced by personal biases, elect a foreperson, discuss to reach unanimous verdict, and not disclose vote counts to court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If jurors need to communicate with the judge they must send a signed note through court staff; jury may continue deliberating while awaiting responses.
